newsitem.title: USA: New heart surgery could replace transplants.
newsitem.headline: New heart surgery could replace transplants.

text.p: A new twist on a revolutionary heart surgery technique developed in Brazil could lead to a cure for many people who would normally need a transplant to survive, heart surgeons said on Tuesday.

They warned that the jury was still out on the long-term benefits of the new technique but said it was promising. The technique combines use of a heart-assist device that helps ailing hearts pump blood and the so-called Batista operation pioneered by Brazilian surgeon Randas J.V. Batista.

Batista, working at a rural hospital in Brazil, found he could improve the function of enlarged hearts, which can cause heart attacks, by cutting away part of the left ventricle and sewing the heart back together.

In July, O.H. Frazier, chief of cardiopulmonary transplantation at the Texas Heart Institute in St. Luke's Hospital, removed the heart-assist device from a patient who had been using it for a year and performed the Batista operation. The results were excellent and the patient is living a normal life, Frazier told a news conference.
"Patients who have been on the heart-assist device may do especially well after the (Batista) operation because their hearts have become stronger and healthier," he said.
Heart surgeon Tomas Salerno, who was the first U.S.-based surgeon to perform the Batista operation, said Frazier's work was a "monumental contribution."

"He demonstrated that if you put the heart at rest (by using an assist device) the cells go back to normal, but the heart is still big. If you can make the heart smaller, you can have a potentially normal heart," he said.
"The assist device could become a bridge to the Batista operation," said Salerno, chief of cardiovascular surgery at Buffalo General Hospital in Buffalo, New York.

Salerno and Batista were in Houston on Tuesday to meet with Frazier. Batista, who developed his procedure because he had no other means of treating patients with enlarged hearts, said he had performed the operation on 420 patients.

He said 40 percent of them had died but the long-term survival rate would be higher at a better-equipped hospital with well-trained staff. Salerno said a mortality rate of 15 to 25 percent would be more likely in a first-rate hospital.

In the United States alone, Batista said, 400,000 heart patients could benefit from his operation, which he developed 13 years ago and began to use regularly only in 1994. "Anybody who has a big, huge heart -- this will help," he said.

The new procedure was greeted skeptically by many heart surgeons but is now being tested around the world. Frazier said he has performed the operation on six patients. One of them died, but the others are doing well.

Still, Frazier warned that it was too early to know if the Batista operation would truly revolutionize heart surgery. "We'll have to wait and see because there have been some (heart rhythm) problems after the surgery," he said.

The procedure is much cheaper than a transplant -- $20,000 vs. $100,000 -- and leaves the patient with alternatives that a transplant does not, he said. "It doesn't burn any bridges. Once you've done a transplant, you've burned all bridges."
